kanji/上.title: 上
kanji/上.content:
上

Above, Up

On: ジョウ, ショウ, シャン
Kun: うえ, -うえ, うわ-, かみ, あ.げる, -あ.げる, あ.がる, -あ.がる, あ.がり, -あ.がり, のぼ.る, のぼ.り, のぼ.せる, のぼ.す, たてまつ.る
Kyūjitai: 丄
Componentes: ⺊, 一

Etimología
From zh sit-pro *tVŋ  top. Cognate with bo སྟེང, bo ཡང་རྩེ  summit; pinnacle (Bodman, 1980), lus zo  to be high, lus zah  to respect; to revere (STEDT).  | Shijing rimes indicate occasional level tone for pronunciation 2 (Schuessler, 2007). | Pronunciation 1 is the exopassive of pronunciation 2 with suffix *-s, literally meaning “what has been raised” (Schuessler, 2007). The rising tone in Middle Chinese words with voiced stop initials regularly evolves into departing tone in Mandarin. Pronunciation 3 results from 叶韻, i.e. its pronunciation has been artificially changed to preserve rhymes in classical poetry.

kanji/下.title: 下
kanji/下.content:

Below, Down, Descend, Give, Low, Inferior

On: カ, ゲ
Kun: した, しも, もと, さ.げる, さ.がる, くだ.る, くだ.り, くだ.す, -くだ.す, くだ.さる, お.ろす, お.りる
Kyūjitai: 丅
Componentes: 一, 卜

Etimología
zh :der sit-pro:*(k/g)la-k/j/t | From zh sit-pro *(k/g)la-k/j/t  to fall (STEDT): | * inside Sinitic, cognate with 落 to fall, to drop, 露 dew, 陊 to collapse and 阤 hillside, slope; | * outside Sinitic, cognate with lus tla ~ tlâk  to fall, lus thla ~ thlâk  to drop, my ကျ  to fall and my ချ  to drop. | Schuessler (2007) instead proposed an zh aav origin by comparing 下 to descend, down, below to km; additionally, he suggested that Sino-Tibetan influence had possibly caused the weakening of foreign final *-k to OC final *-ʔ. He derives the departing tone (*去聲) pronunciation via two derivations: | * 下 to be put down is an exopassive derivation (ibid.); | * 下 to descend, to fall is a later, general departing tone derivative (ibid.).

kanji/不.title: 不
kanji/不.content:
不

Negative, Non-, Bad, Ugly, Clumsy

On: フ, ブ
Kun: —
Kyūjitai: 㐬
Componentes: 一

Etimología
Old Chinese had two sets of negatives: the initial *p-series and the initial *m-series. zh 不 is the prototype of the *p-series of negatives. Although it is the usual Literary Chinese negative attested from the oracle bone script down, its current usage is now confined to Mandarin dialects. In the oracle bone inscriptions, a total of five negative particles can be found: *不, *弗, *毋, *勿 and *非. With the exception of *非 (discussed later), the remaining can be neatly organised into the following system: | {| class=“wikitable” style=“text-align:center” | ! !! *-V !! *-ɯd | |- | ! *p-type negatives ((無) || 勿 | |} | Takashima (1996) argued that the *m-type negatives are modal (i.e. negative verbs which are thought of as controllable by the Shang Dynasty Shang), whereas the *p-type negatives are non-modal (imply uncontrollability; actions which are beyond the control of living persons). | In the p-series, zh 不 usually goes with intransitive verbs in the oracle bone script, and 弗 with transitive ones, although there are some glaring exceptions. Little or no pattern can be discerned in the m-type category. Takashima (1996) also proposed that the difference between the two vowel series was whether they preceded “stative, eventive, passive” (-V series) or “non-stative, non-eventive, active” (-ɯd series) verbs. | It is possible that the two parallel series of negatives in Old Chinese represent a fusion of the common Sino–Tibetan sit-pro *ma  no, not (carried by the eastward-migrating early Sino–Tibetans) and an indigenous negation system in Central China, and that the merger had been complete by the Shang Dynasty Shang times. Compare a similar system in Proto-Tai: tai-pro *ɓawᴮ  not [strong form 1], tai-pro *boːᴮ  not [strong form 2], tai-pro *miːᴬ  not [weak form]; th บ่  (literary, archaic, dialectal) not. | The development from Old Chinese to Middle Chinese was not regular. The character zh 不 replaced zh 弗 (OC *pɯd, MC *piut), to respect the naming taboo for Emperor Zhao of Han, although the pronunciation has remained in nearly all topolects (e.g. Beijing Mandarin bù, Guangzhou Cantonese bat1, Meixian Hakka bud5, Shanghainese Wu peq). The Modern Standard Mandarin pronunciation is also from this checked coda word, but this word escaped from regular sound changes during its evolution to the modern pronunciation bù. The expected reading is fu (tone undetermined), with labiodentalisation. The rising-tone pronunciation had a Middle Chinese homophone *否 not, which is now primarily used in compounds, and demonstrates the regular development into modern f-. Another example of a high-frequency word escaping this sound change is 父 dad, which resulted in the late coinage of the character 爸. | zh 不 is cognate with other negation particles in the *p-type category: | * 弗 not; | * 非 not be; not – can be safely regarded as a fusion of 不 not and 惟 to be; | * 否 not; to be wrong; | * 匪 it is not; to be not; and | * 棐 it is not; to be not. | Cognate with th บ่  (literary, archaic, dialectal) not (Schuessler, 2007).

Cognate with 太 too, excessively, 泰 big. Wang (1982) also lists 誕 big, magniloquent, ridiculous as a cognate, which Schuessler (2007) suggests is cognate with 延 to extend instead. There are no unambiguous Tibeto-Burman cognates. Proto-Tibeto-Burman sit-pro *taj  big, from which came Written Tibetan bo མཐེ་བོ  thumb, nun tʰɛ  big, large, great, Mikir tʰè, ketʰè (“big, large, great”), my တယ်  very, is often compared with. There is no final –s in the Tibeto-Burman words, but a –y, which, according to James Matisoff, “indicates emergent quality in stative verbs”. Also compare Chinese 多 many, much, 都 all, as well as my လတ်, which bears particular resemblance to the Baxter-Sagart reconstruction.

kanji/天.title: 天
kanji/天.content:
天

Heavens, Sky, Imperial

On: テン
Kun: あまつ, あめ, あま-
Kyūjitai: 𠀘
Componentes: 一, 大

Etimología
This character was previously reconstructed to have a /*tʰ/-initial in Old Chinese, but this hypothesis has been largely discounted in recent reconstructions, in light of evidence from early Chinese accounts of dialectal pronunciations, transcription of other languages, as well as cognate/derived characters within Chinese, which has all pointed to a voiceless resonant initial /*l̥-/ in Old Chinese. According to [ctext.org/shi-ming/shi-tian/zh chapter 1] of Shiming, by c. 200 , this initial had already produced dialectal variation in the pronunciation: People in central-western China pronounced it with the back of the tongue, like 顯, while people in eastern China pronounced it with the tip of the tongue, like 坦. An old northwestern dialect variant survives as 祆 God of the Zoroastrians, and the word 天竺 India was used to transcribe Old Persian *Hind-uka (“India”). | Further etymology is unknown. During the time when this term was reconstructed with a /*tʰ-/ initial, it was frequently compared with tengri, the name for God in early Turkic and Mongolic peoples’ languages. This now appears unlikely. The only certain external cognate is the bca - (a language closely related to Chinese) word bca heinl  sky, heaven /xẽ⁵⁵/. Chen (1998) proposes cognation with 祁連 and 赫連, transcriptions of a Xiongnu word for “sky”, which he also relates to 昊天.

Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 扌, 丁

Etimología
This post-classical word (its earliest extant attestation is in Shuowen) was pronounced *teŋ in Late Old Chinese, as would be expected from a *丁 phonetic. By the early Ming dynasty Ming period, the character had been borrowed (訓讀) for another word with the same meaning but a different pronunciation, without the nasal ending. This may be related to the previous reading, as a dialectal variant. In Mandarin and some other varieties, the new reading became standard; however, derivations of the older pronunciation are still used in other varieties such as Wu and Min Nan, as well as Vietnamese (vi đánh). | It has been compared to lus dêng  to throw; to fling; to hammer and proposed to be from zh sit (Schuessler, 2007). Also compare mkh-pro *dah *dah ~ daʔ to hit, to meet, whence mnw ဒး  to hit (a mark), meet with, reach [goal], be correct, apposite, to fit and km ទះ  to slap, to strike. | vi đá, despite superficial semantic and phonetic similarities, as well as Nôm attestations of zh 打 being used to write the Vietnamese term, appears to be unrelated. | The pronunciation da is recorded in zh 六書故 as zh 都假切.

kanji/月.title: 月
kanji/月.content:
月

Month, Moon

On: ゲツ, ガツ
Kun: つき
Kyūjitai: 𡇹
Componentes: 月

Etimología
From zh sit-pro *s-ŋʷ(j)a-t  moon; star, whence also Magar language Magar und , tbq-lob-pro *mwatᴸ (whence lhu məʔkə məʔ-kə), duu gurmet  star (Matisoff, 1980; LaPolla, 1987; STEDT). | Various alternative etymologies have also been proposed: | * Unger (1992) proposes cognation with bo ངོ  waxing and waning moon; half moon (as in bo མར་ངོ  waning moon and bo ཡར་ངོ  waxing moon), which Schuessler (2007) connects to sit-pro *s-ŋow  white; light colour. However, Sagart (1999) points out that the Tibetan word may be analyzed as a derivative of bo ངོ  face, which would mean the semantic connection between “moon” and “face” had to occur either independently in Chinese and Tibetan or in Proto-Sino-Tibetan; it also requires positing a suffix und -t in Chinese. | * Pulleybank (1995a) proposes another etymology based on the glyph for zh 名 (reconstructed as und *màŋʲ), which he analyses as a phono-semantic compound of phonetic zh 夕 and semantic zh 口. He suggests that the phonetic component represents a lost word und *màŋʲ  moon, and reconstructs zh 月 as und *mŋʲ (consonantal frame of “moon”) + und *-at (suffix) > und *ŋʲʷat. However, there are more straightforward ways of explaining the glyph origin of zh 名 (see there), which would nullify the hypothesis of the lost word. | * Related to zh 越 in some way. | ** Mei (1979) derives zh 月 from 越: und **N-gjot > *ngwjat. Also in this proposed word family is 歲 year. The semantics of this word family is centred around “to pass; to elapse”. While Matisoff (1980) seems supportive of this word family, STEDT reconstructs tbq-pro *ɢʷrat *grwat to travel; to go through for zh 越 and zh 歲, separate from the root for zh 月. | ** Ferlus (2012) reconstructs the och - as und *ŋ.wat and puts it in a word family formed from a Chinese root und *wat, having a meaning of “circularity” or “circular boundary”. This proposed word family includes 越, as in “to cross the enclosure of the village”, and 外, as in “out of the enclosure of the village”.

There are many proposed etymologies: | * Sagart and Baxter (2009) compare it to bo གོང་མ  superior one. | * Schuessler (2007) compares it to bo དབང  strength, power and my အန်  strength, power, which derive from zh sit-pro *d-baŋ  strength, power. However, reconstructing the och - as *waŋ, he notes the mismatch between Old Chinese *w- vs. Tibetan *b- (unless *dw- can become db-; for possible *b- ~ * w- variation, see *花). He also compares it to Konyak languages Proto-Northern Naga und *waŋ  chief. | * Schuessler (2007) alternatively proposes a connection to okz vāṅ, okz vaṅ km វាំង, “royal palace”}}, which he considers to be cognate with km ហ្លួង  king. This is perhaps supported by a Chinese bronze inscriptions bronze inscription where zh 王 refers to a place, not the Zhou dynasty Zhou king (Shaughnessy, 1991). The semantic shift from “palace” to “king” parallels egy pr-ꜥꜣ  pharaoh, from egy pr  house + egy ꜥꜣ  great, big. The connection to the okz - word would thus relate it to mkh-pro *waŋ *waŋ ~ *waaŋ enclosure; to go round, which is part of a larger aav word family, including 營  to encamp; to surround and 環  ring. Bodman (1980) connects zh 王 with 皇 sovereign, which Schuessler (2007) connects to this word family. | * Speculations exist about its connection to 尪 lame, crippled and 狂 mad, based on theories about the connection between ancient Chinese kingship and shamanism (Keightley, 1995).

kanji/西.content:
西

West, Spain

On: セイ, サイ, ス
Kun: にし
Kyūjitai: 㢴
Componentes: 一, 𠁤

Etimología
The word is traditionally reconstructed to have a /*s/-initial in Old Chinese, e.g. /*sɯːl/ in Zhengzhang (2003). However, recent scholarship has suggested that the Old Chinese initial should instead be reconstructed as /*s-nˤ/, one of the reasons being *西 appears to be the phonetic in 迺 nǎi, the archaic graphic variant of 乃. The new reconstruction, /*s-nˤər/ in Baxter and Sagart (2014), also accounts for how *西 can be the phonetic in 哂 to smile. For more information, see Sagart (2004), Baxter and Sagart (2014) and Nohara (2018). | In light of the new construction with the initial consonant cluster /*s-nˤ/, the possibilities of the etymology of zh 西, aside from being cognate with 棲 to roost; to rest (B-S OC /*s-nˤər/), include: | * Related to bo ནེར་བ  to sink; to fall gradually (Unger, 1990). | * Related to cdm नेलःसा  to go down; to sink, which may be the same etymon as the Written Tibetan word above (Schuessler, 2007). | * Related to the root 尼 nǐ to stop (OC /*nˤərʔ/ for intransitive form, /*nˤərʔ-s/ for transitive form in Baxter and Sagart (2014)). | * Related to bo མནལ  sleep and my နား  to rest; to stop for a while (Hill, 2019). | * An zh aav - nominal n-infix derivative from the root “go down”, as in omx cnis  ghat  Proto-Sinitic *sn-. If true, then this etymon literally means “the place where one goes down to” > Mon “ghat” > OC “nest, west” and its base form is 濟 via Austroasiatic (Schuessler, 2007).
